hints: Focus on the carbon skeleton first, with two carbons joined by a double bond, where can the two Br atoms go?
Deduction / Stepping Stone: You can put both Br atoms on the same carbon to make 1,1-dibromoethene, or one on each carbon to make 1,2-dibromoethene.
Synthesis / Final Link: Now ask which of those arrangements can show cis-trans isomerism around the restricted C=C bond, and add them all up.
walkthrough:
**Draw the structural possibilities**

Think of ethene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$, and replace two H with Br. There are only two different connectivity patterns.

$$\text{CH}_2=\text{CBr}_2 \text{ (1,1-isomer) and CHBr=CHBr (1,2-isomer)}$$

**Check for cis-trans stereoisomerism**

Remember, rotation about $\text{C=C}$ is restricted, so different spatial arrangements can be locked in. This only matters when each C of the double bond has two different groups.

$$\text{1,1-isomer: C has (H,H) and (Br,Br), no cis-trans. 1,2-isomer: each C has (H,Br), cis-trans possible.}$$

**Count them all up**

The 1,1-isomer gives 1 structure. The 1,2-isomer gives 2 stereoisomers, cis (both Br on same side) and trans (Br on opposite sides).

$$1 + 2 = 3 \text{ total isomers}$$

options.A: 2 counts only the structural isomers (1,1- and 1,2-) but forgets stereoisomerism. The 1,2-arrangement splits into cis and trans forms, so the total is larger.
options.B: 3 is correct: 1 for $\text{CH}_2=\text{CBr}_2$ plus 2 for cis-$\text{CHBr=CHBr}$ and trans-$\text{CHBr=CHBr}$. This covers both structural and stereoisomers.
options.C: 4 is a common overcount. It assumes the 1,1-isomer also has cis and trans forms, but it cannot because one carbon has two identical H atoms and the other has two identical Br atoms.
options.D: 5 is too high and has no basis here. There are no other connectivities like alkynes or rings that are stable isomers of this formula under this alkene pattern, and no extra stereoisomers.
